prize_parts.citation: for pioneering large-volume neutrino telescopes and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: IceCube is a discovery in the sense I care about: a new messenger found in nature rather than an idea waiting for confirmation. A diffuse flux of TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrinos has been established in several independent channels over a decade of data, and the first source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) shows the window is already producing astrophysics on cosmic accelerators. It rests on decades of patient detector development, which the committee has always valued, and it has an existential flavour: these particles carry information from places no photon can escape. A two-person award, Halzen as the driver of the concept and the full-scale detector, Spiering as the pioneer of the Baikal and early neutrino-telescope programme, is the cleanest attribution available on this shortlist for a large-collaboration observation. I have moved my first place from the Higgs experiments to this because, after reading colleagues, I think the Higgs attribution problem is less tractable than I allowed in my opening.
statement.case_against: Source identification is still at the 3-4 sigma level for individual objects, so the picture of where the neutrinos come from is incomplete and the field may look very different in five years; a cautious committee could argue the discovery of the flux is secure but the physics story is early. The 2002 prize (Davis, Koshiba) already covered cosmic neutrinos, and Baikal, DUMAND, AMANDA and ANTARES pioneers could reasonably claim a place, so Halzen and Spiering may be criticised as an incomplete or arbitrary selection. Opening support is thin (three members ranked it), and my own ballot ranked the Higgs experiments first on scientific significance alone, which is larger than anything else on the list.

responses.point: Ranked IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery that took decades of detector development, with a solid diffuse flux but individual-source evidence below 5 sigma, and flagged the 2002 neutrino prize and uncertain credit for AMANDA/Baikal/DUMAND founders.
responses.response: I agree on the instrument-driven character and on the diffuse flux being the stable core; that is exactly why I would frame the citation around the discovery of the flux and the telescopes, not around source identification, which keeps the sub-5-sigma sources from carrying weight they cannot bear. I disagree that the 2002 prize is a serious obstacle: Davis and Koshiba detected solar and supernova neutrinos at MeV energies, a different messenger regime from PeV neutrinos of extragalactic origin. The founder question is real. I would want the expert reports to say whether Spiering's Baikal and DUMAND-era role is as decisive as Halzen's, because if it is not, the pairing weakens.

responses.point: Ranked the Higgs experiments fifth and IceCube seventh; she notes that the three Higgs names are detector leaders rather than the people who did the discovery analyses, and that IceCube recognition is arguably early because sources are not fully identified.
responses.response: Your point about the Higgs names is the strongest argument against my own first choice, and it moved me: a prize for detector leadership of ATLAS and CMS is not the same as a prize for the discovery, and naming Gianotti and Incandela instead would be a different award. On IceCube being early I disagree in part. The existence of the astrophysical flux is established, and the committee has awarded discoveries before the full interpretation was in, so source identification is a qualification and not a reason to wait. I would concede that if sources stay at 3-4 sigma, we should word the citation conservatively.

responses.point: Ranked optical lattice clocks first: a measurement breakthrough with thorough independent confirmation, a natural Katori-Ye pairing and good timing, with the risk that earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes make it look incremental.
responses.response: The attribution for Katori and Ye is indeed clean and the maturity is not in doubt, so I take B042 seriously and keep it as an alternative. My reservation is the one you raise yourself: after 2005 and 2012 the committee may ask whether lattice clocks are a discovery or a very refined instrument, and I would put more weight on a new window on nature than on another factor of ten in precision. I would not resist it if the committee prefers the metrology line, and the redefinition of the second would give it a natural anchor.

responses.point: Ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as theory anticipating a new quantum state, with a clean split between Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero and reproduction by many groups, though the superconducting mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: This is the sort of exchange between prediction and experiment I admire, and I ranked it seventh mainly because I think the field is still early. My worry is that the pairing mechanism remains debated, and the credit for the experimental discovery extends to Yuan Cao and others who cannot be named under the three-person limit. If the committee wants a condensed-matter prize this year I would not oppose B019, but I would want a few more years of settled interpretation before placing it above an observational discovery.

uncertainties: Whether Spiering's role is as decisive as Halzen's relative to other early large-volume neutrino-telescope leaders, and whether outside experts would name someone else.
Whether the 3-4 sigma status of individual neutrino sources makes the committee want to wait, or whether the established diffuse flux is sufficient.
Whether the committee can justify the Higgs experiments (my opening first place) given that the three credited names are detector leaders and not the discovery analysts.
How much the committee wants a discovery of nature this year as opposed to a metrology or condensed-matter prize, given limited support for B032 so far.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: my connections are Gross (PhD supervisor), Rubinstein (deceased), Van Riet, and the Uppsala string-theory group, none of whom is credited on any shortlisted ballot. As Secretary I commission outside evaluations and will be careful to separate that role from my advocacy.
